answer.evidence: The structured first-layer units fall into two families. The first family, 'ring' units 0, 1, 18, 19, 20, 22 and 29, has a negative core around rows 11-12, cols 10-12. Each has a strong positive annulus at roughly radius 3-6 (rows 5-18, cols 5-18), with negative weights further out. These units feed layer-2 units u10 and u12 with large positive weights (e.g. 84, 99, 86, 89, 70 into u10). u10 and u12 have positive output weights (+74, +47), so a filled annulus, meaning a large blob, pushes toward class 1. The second family, 'inverse' units 14, 15, 23 and 27, has a positive centre (rows 10-13, cols 10-13, up to 99), a negative ring and a high bias. These units feed u1, u6, u8 and u9, which have output weights of -87, -89, -65 and -76, so a bright centre with a dark ring, meaning a small blob, pushes toward class 0. Unit 8 is a broadly positive brightness unit feeding u3 and u10 (toward class 1), which is consistent with total blob area. No compact region carries a consistent off-centre weight block of the kind a patch or corner-marker shortcut would produce. Corners and borders hold mostly background-level weights. There are scattered isolated pixels with large, sign-mirrored weights across the two families, e.g. (1,16-17), (8,2), (3,5), (3,12), (16,21), (20,19), (19,2), (23,11) and (0,11). These are single pixels spread over the whole frame with mixed directions, not a coherent localized feature. They look like overfitting to background noise rather than a deliberate spurious cue. The uncertainty in this verdict comes from those pixels.
answer.main_feature: The model compares activation in a central disk against an annulus around it. Brightness in the surrounding ring (radius ~4-6 px) drives class 1 (large blob); brightness confined to the centre with a dark ring drives class 0 (small blob).
